body.p: This responds to the Final Office Action dated May 9, 2023. Claims 20, 21, 24, 82-84, 87, and 91 are amended. Claims 1-19 and 26-78 were previously canceled without disclaimer or prejudice. As a result, claims 20-25 and 79-92 are now pending in this application.

The undersigned would like to thank Examiners Joseph A. Tombers and Patrick Fernandes for the courtesies extended during the telephone interview of August 9, 2023. The interview was attended by the undersigned representative and by Attorney Justin Leisey (Reg. No. 65,082) asrepresentative for the Applicant. During the interview, distinctions over the cited references were discussed. Examiner Tombers acknowledged these distinctions and agreed to review the formal response as-filed.
Claims 24, 83-85 and 89-92 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being
unpatentable over U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2012/0078071 by Bohm (hereinafter "Bohm") in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2011/0144463 by Pesach (hereinafter "Pesach").

Claims 20, 22-23, 79-82 and 86-88 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Bohm in view of Pesach and U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2016/0151010 by Erez (hereinafter "Erez").
Claim 21 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Bohm in view of Pesach and U.S. Patent No. 5,918,590 by Burkett (hereinafter "Burkett").

Claim 25 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Bohm Sebastian in view of Pesach, Erez, and U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2016/0058380 by Lee (hereinafter "Lee").
Aprimafacie determination of obviousness requires a factual showing that "the subject
matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having

ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains."1 The question of obviousness is resolved on the basis of underlying factual determinations including (1) "the scope and content of the prior art," (2) "differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art," (3) "the level of ordinary skill in the art," and (4) where in evidence, "secondary considerations."2 Here, no prima facie determination of obviousness is properly established for at least the reason that the scope and content of the cited references, even if combined, do not teach or suggest all claim elements, or support rational inferences that a person skilled in the art reasonably would employ to reach all claim elements, at least as set forth below.
APPLICATION OF 103 TO THE REJECTED CLAIMS
First, claim 20 has been amended to recite:
sensor electronics hardware, wherein the sensor electronics hardware is configured to perform operations comprising:
detecting that the implantable analyte sensor has been inserted into the host, and

responsive to detecting insertion of the implantable analyte sensor into the host, providing power to the first heating element, the providing of the power to the first heating element being while the implantable analyte sensor is inserted into the host. None of the cited references teach or suggest at least these features. The Office asserts that claim 20 is obvious over Bohm, Pesach, and Erez. See Office Action at p. 10. The Office admits that "Bohm fails to disclose a first heating element included in the adhesive pad and positioned to provide heat to the skin surface of the host when the implantable analyte sensor is inserted into the host" and that "Bohm and Pesach fail to disclose responsive to detecting insertion of the implantable analyte sensor into the host, providing power to the first heating element." See Office Action at pp. 11, 12. The Office goes on to cite Erez as purportedly disclosing this feature. See id.
Erez discloses a "blood sampling device" that involves piercing the skin of a host with a needle. See Erez at Abstract. Erez fails to disclose or suggest "providing power to the first heating
2 Graham v. John Deere, 383 U.S. 1, 17-18, 148 U.S.P.Q. 459, 467; KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex, Inc.,
550 U.S. 398, 406-7, 82 U.S.P.Q.2d 1385, 1390 (2007), cited in Ex parte Frye, Appeal No. 2009- 006013 (BPAI 2010) (precedential).

This is not what is recited by claim 20, however. "Retraction of the piercing element" is not an insertion of an implantable analyte sensor. Indeed, even if one considers Erez's non-sensor "piercing element" to meet the recited "implantable analyte sensor," which Applicant does not concede, Erez still fails to meet the above-referenced features. Indeed, the retraction disclosed by Erez is the opposite of insertion. Further, any activation of a heating element that is "upon retraction of the piercing element," as disclosed by Erez does not occur "while the implantable sensor is inserted into the host," as recited by claim 1.
For at least these reasons, Applicant submits that there is no prima facia obviousness of claim 20 or of claims 22, 23, 79-82, and 86-88 that depend directly or indirectly from claim 20.
Second, claim 24 has been amended to recite:
a sensor electronics unit installable to the sensor mounting unit, wherein the sensor electronics unit is configured to begin
providing power to the first heating element after being installed to
the sensor mounting unit, the providing of the power to the first
heating element being while the implantable analyte sensor is inserted
into the host.

The references also fail to teach or suggest at least these features. Neither Erez, Pesach, nor Bohm teach or suggest "providing power to the first heating element" where "the providing of power to the first heating element [is] while the implantable analyte sensor is inserted into the host," as recited by claim 24.
For at least these reasons, Applicant submits that there is no prima facia obviousness of claim 24 or of claims 89-92 that depend directly or indirectly from claim 24.
Third, Applicant has herein amended claim 21 to recite:
a first heating element included in the adhesive pad and positioned to provide heat to the skin surface of the host when the
implantable analyte sensor is inserted into the host, at least a portion

of the first heating element being positioned outside a perimeter of the senor mounting unit, and the first heating element comprising at least a first reactant that reacts in the presence of air to generate heat.

The cited references fail to disclose at least these features. The Office cites Pesach as purportedly disclosing the configuration of the recited "first heating element." See Office Action at p. 18. As the Office points out, Pesach discloses at FIG. 2C "a heating element 834 ... coated with a biocompatible adhesive layer coding 816 on its bottom side covered with laminate 818." See Office Action at p. 18, Pesach at FIG. 2C, 130. However, the heating element 834 does not extend beyond a perimeter of the disposable portion 810. See Pesach at FIGS. 2B-2D. It is certainly not the case that the heating element 834 of Pesach comprises "at least a portion," that is "positioned outside a perimeter of the sensor mounting unit," as recited by claim 21.
For at least these reasons, Applicant submits that there is no prima facia obviousness of claim 21.
Fourth, claim 83 has been amended to recite:
wherein the sensor electronics hardware is configured to perform operations comprising:

detecting that the analyte sensor has been inserted into a host, providing power to the heating element, and in response to determining that a signal generated by the analyte sensor is substantially linear, ceasing to provide power to the heating element.

The Office admits that Bohm fails to disclose the recited "heating element." See Office Action at p. 7. The Office goes on to assert that Pesach discloses, "in response to determining that a response of the analyte sensor is substantially linear, ceasing to provide power to the heating element." See Office Action at p. 7.

Even if the Examiner's analysis of Pesach is correct, which Applicant does not concede, Pesach fails to teach or suggest any arrangement that includes "ceasing to provide power to the heating element" that is "in response to determining that a signal generated by the analyte sensor is substantially linear," as recited by claim 83. Pesach fails to disclose or suggest any controlling of a heating element that is in response to any reaction of an analyte sensor, let alone "in response to
determining that a signal generated by the analyte sensor is substantially linear," as recited by claim 83.
For at least these reasons, Applicant submits that there is no prima facia obviousness of claim 83 or of claims 84 and 85 that depend from claim 83.

In the interest of clarity and brevity, every assertion made in the Office Action may not have been equally addressed. Silence regarding any such assertion does not constitute any admission or acquiescence. All rights not exercised in connection with this response, such as the right to challenge or rebut any tacit or explicit characterization of any reference or of any of the present claims, the right to challenge or rebut any asserted factual or legal basis of any of the rejections, the right to swear behind any cited reference such as provided under 37 C.F.R. § 1.131 or otherwise, or the right to assert co-ownership of any cited reference, are reserved. It is not admitted that any of the cited references or any other references of record are relevant to the present claims, or that they constitute prior art. To the extent that any rejection or assertion is based upon the Examiner's personal knowledge, rather than any objective evidence of record as manifested by a cited prior art reference, timely objection to such reliance on Official Notice is made, and all rights to request that the Examiner provide a reference or affidavit in support of such assertion, as required by MPEP § 2144.03, are reserved. All rights to pursue any cancelled claims in a subsequent patent application claiming the benefit of priority of the present patent application, and to request rejoinder of any withdrawn claim, as required by MPEP § 821.04, are likewise reserved.

It is respectfully submitted that the claims are in condition for allowance, and notification to that effect is earnestly requested. The Examiner is invited to telephone the undersigned at (612) 224-3774 to facilitate prosecution of this application.
If necessary, please charge any additional fees or deficiencies, or credit any overpayments to Deposit Account No. 19-0743.
